_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version. Ticket numbers kept from the brief (4417, 4471); the earlier wrong pairs are 4528 and 4582, 4739 and 4793, 5106 and 5160, all inside the shop's live ticket range. The brief's "empty the cache every night at closing" becomes "at every shift change": the shop never closes.
title: Asking Twice Costs Twice

post.author: u/night_counter_ilinca
post.title: I'm the night clerk at a pawnshop that never closes. At 02:20 our assistant told a woman her grandmother's ring was a brass carriage clock. The clock is on another ticket.

blocks.text: I'm Ilinca, night clerk at Bexendale's, a pawnshop open day and night. People leave something valuable with us and borrow money against it. Each loan gets a numbered line in our receipt book and a matching paper ticket. A loan runs four months; after its last day, we may sell the item. My shift is 20:00 to 08:00.

Customers text us questions, and an assistant answers. Behind it is a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back. A company called a provider runs it and bills us for every bit of text it reads or writes.
Those bits are called tokens. With every question, the app sends our shop policy, 9,000 tokens of rules. If the question names a ticket, it also sends that ticket's line from the receipt book.

Paying twice for the same answer annoyed Mr Cosgrave, our manager. Three weeks ago he added a store of saved answers, each kept 24 hours, like a spike of old receipts by the till. A store like that is called a cache.

It works in steps. First, the app turns the new question into an embedding: a list of numbers that stands for what it means. Next, it compares that with every saved question, giving each a similarity score, where 1 means the same meaning.

If the best score reaches a cut-off, the app sends that saved answer and never asks the model. The cut-off is called the threshold, and a saved answer sent is a hit. Otherwise the model answers, and its answer is saved.

For three weeks the threshold was 0.95, and his screen showed 12 hits in every 100 questions. On Monday at 09:00 he lowered it to 0.90 to cut the bill, and emptied the cache to start clean. Since then: 31 in 100.

He also read about prompt caching: the provider keeps the long part that never changes, our policy, ready for a while, so sending it again costs about a tenth. But saving it costs a quarter extra and lasts five minutes. At night our texts come further apart, so he left it off.
Here is the app's record from tonight. Each line shows the time, then the question, the answer, or what the app did.

21:05  When is the last day to collect ticket 4417?
21:05  closest saved: 0.84. Asked the model.
21:05  The last day to collect the brass carriage clock
       is Monday 2 November.   (saved)
02:20  When is the last day to collect ticket 4471?
02:20  closest saved: 21:05, score 0.93. Sent it.
At 02:21 she texted back: There is no clock. It is my grandmother's ring.

Mrs Nwachukwu was at the counter by 03:00, ticket in hand. Line 4471: one gold ring, pawned 9 July, last day Monday 9 November. Fifty-four lines up, 4417: a brass carriage clock, last day 2 November. What else a stranger's saved answer might have told her is a worry for another night.

At 02:20 the question about ticket 4471 scores 0.93 against it, over the 0.90 threshold, and the saved answer about the brass carriage clock is sent.

blocks.text: The two questions differ only by two swapped digits. Mr Cosgrave searched the cache's log since Monday and found three more answers about the wrong ticket. Nobody had complained. The assistant answers again tonight. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Bexendale's is haunted, though a clock answering for a ring comes close. A cache can match a new question in two ways. One is exact match: only the very same words, letter for letter, like a coat hook that takes only its own cloakroom ticket. The other is by meaning, as yours does, scoring how alike two questions are; that kind is called a semantic cache. Three questions. Word for word, how did the 21:05 and 02:20 questions differ? Since Monday, how many hits were there, and how many answered about a different ticket? And what do two questions about the same ticket score, against two whose numbers swap digits?

replies.author: u/night_counter_ilinca
replies.text: Only the digits: 4417 and 4471, every other word the same. Since Monday the log holds 300 questions and 93 hits. Four answered about another ticket, each a pair whose numbers swap two digits: Tuesday 16:10, ticket 4582 got 4528's answer, at 0.92; Wednesday 22:45, 4793 got 4739's, at 0.94; Thursday 13:50, 5160 got 5106's, at 0.91; and tonight's, at 0.93. Two questions about the same ticket in other words score 0.90 to 0.99 in our log, and the same words twice score 1.00. Questions about tickets whose numbers differ in other ways score 0.88 or less.

comments.author: u/safe_line_corbishley
comments.text: 0.90 was just greedy. 0.95 is the safe line everyone uses, and your own log shows why: the swapped tickets top out at 0.94, so at 0.95 they can never match. You had three quiet weeks at 0.95 to prove it. Put the number back where it was and every clock stays on its own ticket.

replies.author: u/night_counter_ilinca
replies.text: Mr Cosgrave says the bill goes back up with it, but he'd rather pay than have another night like this one.

comments.author: u/fresh_each_shift_ondrasek
comments.text: Saved answers shouldn't outlive the shift that made them. Empty the whole cache at 08:00 and 20:00, when the clerks change over. Every shift starts clean, and nothing old is left lying about to be handed to the wrong person.

reply.prompt: The assistant answers again tonight. What should Bexendale's change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the match threshold back to 0.95, so ticket numbers can no longer match each other.
options.verdict: Safer tickets, the bill back, and still a wrong match
options.part2: Mr Cosgrave set the threshold back to 0.95 and replayed the week's 300 questions. 36 hits, 12%, as in the first three weeks, and no answer about another ticket: the swapped pairs top out at 0.94. The cost per question went back up from 0.69 of a full call, one question sent to the model with the whole policy, to 0.88. Then he typed two questions that matter at night: Can I pawn my ring tonight? and Can I pawn my ring tomorrow? New loans need our valuer, the person who prices what we take, and she works 09:00 to 17:00, so the right answers are no and yes. The two score 0.96. The second got the first one's saved answer: not tonight.
options.senior: A threshold is one number for every kind of question, and a similarity score measures how alike two texts are, not whether their answers are the same. Swapped digits score 0.91 to 0.94; tonight and tomorrow score 0.96. Any line you draw either lets some wrong pairs through or throws away good hits, and raising it buys safety only by giving up the saving. GPTCache's README warns that a semantic cache can give false positives on hits and false negatives on misses. Decide by what a wrong answer costs: questions tied to one ticket or one person should not be matched by meaning at all.

options.text: Cache only exact repeats of a question, so no answer is ever sent for a different one.
options.part2: Mr Cosgrave switched the cache to exact repeats only and replayed the week. 9 hits in 300, 3%. Nothing answered about another ticket, and the ring questions both went to the model and got the right answers. The cost per question, 1.00 of a full call with no cache at all, fell only to 0.97: people almost never type the same words twice.
options.senior: Exact matching is the right tool for answers tied to one record, as long as the key, the label an answer is saved under, holds everything that changes the answer: the words and the ticket number. For everything else it gives up most of the saving. GPTCache's README says the same thing: an exact match approach is less effective for model caches, because people word the same question in many ways. Use exact keys where a wrong answer is costly, then look for the money elsewhere. Here, 9,000 of every full call's 10,000 units are the policy, sent with every question.

options.text: Empty the whole cache at every shift change, so no saved answer is older than 12 hours.
options.verdict: Fresher answers, the same wrong ones
options.part2: Mr Cosgrave set the cache to empty at 08:00 and 20:00 and replayed the week. 72 hits, 24%, and three answers about another ticket: Tuesday's 4582, Thursday's 5160 and tonight's 4471. Tonight's 21:05 and 02:20 sit inside one night shift, so emptying at 20:00 and 08:00 never separated them. Only Wednesday's 4793, asked at 22:45 about a question from 18:30, was spared, because the cache was emptied at 20:00 in between. The cost per question rose from 0.69 to 0.76 of a full call, one question sent to the model with the whole policy.
options.senior: How long an answer is kept, its TTL (time to live) from Dead Letter s2e04, decides how out of date it can get. It does nothing about whether the answer belongs to the question. Tonight's pair was five hours and a quarter apart; Tuesday's, four and a half. A shorter life cuts good hits along with bad ones and leaves the matching rule exactly as it was. Use a short life for answers that go stale, like today's gold price, and a different key for answers that belong to one person.

options.text: Never reuse an answer for a named ticket; cache the long shop policy to save money.
options.part2: Mr Cosgrave split the questions. One that names a ticket now uses an exact key: the same words and the same ticket number, or no match. General shop questions keep the meaning match at 0.90. Replayed, the week gave 75 hits, 25%, and no answer about another ticket. At 02:20, 4471 went to the model, which read her line and answered: the gold ring, last day Monday 9 November. Then he turned on prompt caching for the policy. Counting one question sent to the model with the whole policy as a full call: with the five-minute life, 178 of the 225 model calls found the saved policy gone and paid the quarter extra to save it again: 0.76 of a full call per question, no better than without it. With the one-hour life, which costs twice the normal price to save, 201 calls read the policy at a tenth and 24 saved it: 0.28 of a full call per question, against 0.69 for the 0.90 threshold alone.
options.senior: Ask two things of anything you cache. Could the saved answer be wrong for the next person? Then its key must hold everything that changes the answer, here the ticket number, and a meaning match must never stand in for it. And where is the money? Here it was the 9,000-token policy, nine tenths of every full call, so caching that fixed start saves far more than matching more questions by meaning. Anthropic's page says cache reads cost 0.1 times the base input price, five-minute writes 1.25 times and one-hour writes 2 times, and that hits need 100% identical prompt segments. Count the gaps between your calls before you pick the life: at this shop's pace, five minutes saved nothing. Meaning-based matching still can't tell tonight from tomorrow, so keep it to general answers where a near miss does no harm.

sim.title: Replay the week through the cache
sim.lede: You're Mr Cosgrave, replaying the 300 questions texted to Bexendale's from Monday 09:00, when the threshold went to 0.90 and the cache was emptied, to Friday 02:20. No real model runs here. For each question the shop's log gives its closest earlier question and their similarity score; two questions about different tickets are never the same answer. A hit sends the saved answer; when nothing matches, the model answers and its answer is saved, and that is a miss. A full call to the model costs 1.00: the 9,000-token policy, about 250 tokens of question and ticket line, and about 150 tokens of answer at five times the input price, 10,000 units in all. With prompt caching, a call within the cache's life of the last call reads the policy at 0.1 (0.19 of a full call); otherwise it saves the policy again at 1.25 for a five-minute life (1.225) or 2 for a one-hour life (1.90). One rule saves ticket answers under an exact key: a label built from the same words and the ticket number, so only that ticket's own question finds it. Below the table, two test questions, Can I pawn my ring tonight? and Can I pawn my ring tomorrow?, score 0.96 and need opposite answers. You open at Monday 09:00, with nothing replayed.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Replay the week and read 93 hits, 31%, and four answers about another ticket, tonight's 4471 at 0.93 among them. Set the threshold to 0.95: 12%, and the two ring questions still match at 0.96. Try exact repeats only (3%), and emptying at each shift change (tonight's pair survives). Then try exact keys for named tickets with prompt caching off, five minutes and one hour, and play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the shop remembered a clock. The cache matched the 02:20 question about ticket 4471 to the 21:05 question about 4417 at 0.93, over the 0.90 threshold set on Monday, and sent the saved answer. Questions that differ only by swapped digits score 0.91 to 0.94, so at the old 0.95 they never could match.

steps.title: A meaning-based cache, step by step.
steps.text: It is cache-aside, from Dead Letter s2e04: look in the cache first, and on a miss ask the source and keep a copy. First the app turns the new question into an embedding with an embedding model (a1e04). Second it compares that embedding with every question saved in the last 24 hours and takes the highest similarity score. Third, if that score is at least the threshold, it sends the saved answer and the model is never asked. Fourth, if not, it asks the model, sends the answer and saves it with the question. What can go wrong: step three trusts that alike questions have the same answer. For general shop questions they usually do. For a question about one ticket, the answer belongs to that ticket alone.

steps.title: Why 4417 and 4471 look alike.
steps.text: An embedding stands for what a text is about. When is the last day to collect ticket 4417? and the same with 4471 are about the same thing, a last day for a ticket, and differ in two digits that make up a sliver of the text. In this shop's embedding model such pairs score 0.91 to 0.94; two questions about the same ticket in other words score 0.90 to 0.99. The ranges overlap, so no single threshold keeps every good pair and drops every bad one. At 0.95 the week gives 36 hits in 300, 12%, and no ticket mix-ups; at 0.90, 93 hits, 31%, and four. And Can I pawn my ring tonight? against tomorrow? scores 0.96 with opposite answers. What can go wrong: a threshold that looks safe on three quiet weeks is only safe for the pairs those weeks happened to contain.

steps.title: What must never share an answer.
steps.text: Anything tied to one person or one record: a ticket's item, its last day, what is owed. For those, use an exact key, the label an answer is saved under, built from the same words and the ticket number, so only that ticket's own question can find it. Keep meaning-based matching for general questions, like opening hours, where a near match gives the same answer. Replayed that way, the week gives 75 hits, 25%, and no answer about another ticket. A wrong answer here is also someone's private details reaching a stranger; that is the subject of What It Told the Stranger, in Season 7. What can go wrong: a general answer can still depend on the day, as the ring pair shows.

steps.title: Prompt caching the policy, step by step.
steps.text: First, the app marks where the fixed part of its request ends, here after the 9,000-token policy. Second, on the first call the provider saves everything up to that mark; that save costs 1.25 times the normal input price for a five-minute life, or 2 times for one hour. Third, a later call whose start is 100% identical, sent within the life, reads the saved part at 0.1 times the input price, and each read starts the life again. Fourth, a call after the life has run out, or with any change in the fixed part, saves it again at the higher price. Anthropic's page also sets a minimum length, 512 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model; 9,000 clears all of them. What can go wrong: a changing word near the start, like the date or the customer's name, breaks every match after it.

steps.title: When it pays: count the gaps.
steps.text: A full call here is 10,000 units: 9,000 for the policy, 250 for the question and ticket line, and 750 for a 150-token answer at five times the input price. A call that reads the policy costs 900 + 1,000 = 1,900 units; one that saves it costs 11,250 + 1,000 = 12,250 (five minutes) or 18,000 + 1,000 = 19,000 (one hour). With exact ticket keys, 225 of the week's 300 questions reach the model. At five minutes, only 47 came soon enough after the last call to read; 178 saved again, 226.98 full calls against 225 with caching off. At one hour, 201 read and 24 saved: 83.79 full calls, 0.28 a question. What can go wrong: on quiet nights even an hour runs out, so check your own gaps before you count the saving.

diagram.aria: The fix. A customer's text arrives and the app asks: does it name a ticket? If yes, it looks for an exact key, the same words and the same ticket number. If no, it looks for a meaning match among general questions at 0.90. Either way, a miss goes to the model, whose 9,000-token policy is read from the provider's one-hour prompt cache.

explain.caption: Read top left to right. A question that names a ticket can only find an answer saved under the same words and the same ticket number, so 4471 never meets 4417's answer. General questions keep the meaning match at 0.90. A miss on either path goes to the model, and the 9,000-token policy at the start of every call is read from the provider's one-hour cache at a tenth of the price.

fix.title: The fix: exact keys for anything tied to one ticket, and cache the policy instead
fix.text: Sort every question before the cache sees it. If it names a ticket or a customer, look only for an exact key built from the same words and the ticket number; never let a meaning match answer it. Keep the meaning match, at 0.90 or wherever your own labelled pairs say, for general shop questions whose answers don't depend on who asks. Then go after the real cost: put the 9,000-token policy first in every request, mark the end of that fixed part, and turn on prompt caching with a life that fits your gaps; here, one hour. Keep anything that changes, the date, the ticket line, the question, after the mark. Log every hit with the two questions and their score, and check a sample by hand each week, so a wrong match is found by the shop and not by a customer at 02:20.

limits: Meaning-based matching still can't tell tonight from tomorrow: the ring pair scores 0.96 with opposite answers. Keep it to general answers where a near match does no harm, and test it on labelled pairs of questions whose answers you know.
Prompt caching only pays when calls come close together. At this shop's pace the five-minute life cost slightly more than no caching; on a very quiet week even the one-hour life would save little.
Sorting questions by whether they name a ticket depends on spotting the ticket. A customer who writes my ring instead of a number needs the app to ask for it, not a guess.

head: Plan
Hits in the week
Answers about another ticket
Cost per question

The same, policy cached for five minutes
The same, policy cached for one hour

explain.seniorTake: Caching a model's answers is worth doing, but first ask what the answer belongs to. If it belongs to one person or one record, a ticket, an order, an account, the cache key must hold that identity, and only an exact key will do: a similarity score measures how alike two questions read, not whether they share an answer, and numbers that matter are a sliver of the text. Keep meaning-based matching for general questions where a near match gives the same answer, set its threshold from labelled pairs, and log every hit with both questions and the score so mistakes are found by you. Then look at where the tokens actually go. A long fixed policy or instruction block sent with every request is usually most of the bill, and prompt caching it costs a little more on the first call and about a tenth after, as long as calls come within the cache's life. Count the gaps between your calls before choosing that life.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: what a cached start costs
realWorld.text: Anthropic's prompt caching page says 5-minute cache write tokens are 1.25 times the base input tokens price, 1-hour cache write tokens are 2 times the base input tokens price, and cache read tokens are 0.1 times the base input tokens price, with per-model exceptions listed in a footnote, where some newer models read at less.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: five minutes, refreshed on every use
realWorld.text: The page says: By default, the cache has a 5-minute lifetime. The cache is refreshed for no additional cost each time the cached content is used. It adds that the lifetime is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the cache entry.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: identical, and long enough
realWorld.text: Under exact matching the page says cache hits require 100% identical prompt segments, including all text and images up to and including the block marked with cache control. It also lists a minimum cacheable length for each model, from 512 to 4,096 tokens.

realWorld.title: GPTCache: a semantic cache for model answers
realWorld.text: Zilliz's open-source GPTCache describes itself as a semantic cache for storing LLM responses. Its README says GPTCache employs embedding algorithms to convert queries into embeddings and uses a vector store for similarity search, then decides from the similarity whether a request matches the cache.

realWorld.title: GPTCache: false positives, and why not exact match
realWorld.text: The same README warns: In a semantic cache, you may encounter false positives during cache hits and false negatives during cache misses. It also argues that using an exact match approach for LLM caches is less effective due to the complexity and variability of LLM queries, which is the trade this case makes for general questions only.

asked: How would you cache model answers?
interview.answer: I'd split it into two caches with different jobs. For answers, I sort requests first. Anything tied to one user or one record, an order, a balance, a ticket, gets an exact key that includes that identity, or isn't cached at all, because a similarity score says how alike two questions read, not whether they share an answer: order 81530 and 81503 look nearly the same to an embedding. General questions can use a semantic cache, embedding the question and serving a saved answer above a threshold, but I set that threshold from labelled pairs, log every hit with both questions and the score, and keep a short TTL for answers that go stale. For cost, I look at the tokens: a long fixed system prompt or policy sent on every request is usually most of the bill. Prompt caching puts that fixed part first and marks its end; the first call pays a little more to save it, later calls read it at about a tenth, as long as they arrive within its life, five minutes by default on Anthropic's API, refreshed on each use, or an hour at a higher write price. So prompt caching pays when the same prefix comes back within the life: I count the gaps between calls before I pick one, and I keep anything that changes, dates, names, the question, after the cached part.

terms.def: A shop that lends money against something valuable you leave there. Pay back the loan and its interest by the last day and you get it back; after that, the shop may sell it.
Bexendale's numbered book of loans: one line per item, with what it is, when it was pawned and its last day. The paper ticket carries the same number.
The numbered paper a customer keeps for a pawned item, matching a line in the receipt book. Ticket 4471 is Mrs Nwachukwu's gold ring.
The last day to collect a pawned item by paying back the loan. Bexendale's loans run four months: ticket 4471's last day is Monday 9 November.
The person at Bexendale's who prices what customers bring in. New loans need her, and she works 09:00 to 17:00.
When one clerk hands over to the next. Bexendale's shifts change at 08:00 and 20:00; Ilinca works the night shift.
A program that reads text and writes text back, one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01).
A company that runs language models and sells their use, billed by the token (a1e03).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads or writes and is billed by (a1e03).
Bexendale's 9,000 tokens of rules on interest, ID, what it takes and the valuer's hours, sent with every question so the model answers by them.
This case's unit of cost: one question sent to the model with the whole policy, 10,000 units of input price. A cache hit costs no call.
What a provider charges for each token you send and each token it writes back. Output usually costs more; this case uses output at five times input (a1e03).
A store of saved answers kept close at hand so the same question need not be worked out again, like a spike of old receipts by the till (s2e04).
Look in the cache first; on a miss, ask the real source and keep a copy in the cache (s2e04, The Jar on the Counter).
A question answered from the cache, with no model call. A miss is the opposite: the model answers, and its answer is saved.
Hits divided by all questions, as a percentage (s2e04). Bexendale's went from 12% to 31% when the threshold went from 0.95 to 0.90.
A list of numbers that stands for what a text means, made so that texts about the same thing get similar lists (a1e04).
A program that turns text into embeddings. Bexendale's cache runs every question through one before comparing (a1e04).
A number for how alike two embeddings are: 1 for the same meaning, lower for less alike. Cosine similarity is the usual kind (a1e04).
A cut-off on a score above which a program decides something; here, sends a saved answer. A guess until checked on examples whose answers are known (a1e04).
A cache that matches a new question to saved ones by meaning, through embeddings and a similarity threshold, instead of by exact words.
Matching only the very same words, letter for letter, like a coat hook that takes only its own cloakroom ticket.
The label a cache saves an answer under and looks it up by. An exact key for a ticket question holds the words and the ticket number.
A match that shouldn't have happened: here, a hit that sends the answer to a different question. A false negative is a good match missed.
Short for time to live: how long a saved item may be used before it must be fetched again (s2e04). Bexendale's answers live 24 hours.
A provider saving the fixed start of your requests, such as a long policy, so later requests that begin the same way are read at about a tenth of the input price.
In prompt caching, the call that saves the fixed start. Anthropic charges 1.25 times the input price for a five-minute life and 2 times for one hour.
In prompt caching, a call that finds the fixed start already saved and pays 0.1 times the input price for it on most models.
How long a provider keeps a saved start: five minutes by default on Anthropic's API, refreshed each time it is read, or one hour at a higher write price.
The start of a request, up to a point you mark. Prompt caching saves a prefix and matches only one that is 100% identical.
Mr Cosgrave's two test questions, Can I pawn my ring tonight? and Can I pawn my ring tomorrow? They score 0.96 and need opposite answers.
An AI company that makes the Claude models and documents its prompt caching prices and limits.
An open-source semantic cache for model answers from Zilliz, a company that makes vector database software.
A store built to keep embeddings and quickly find the ones closest to a new one. GPTCache uses one for its similarity search.
Short for large language model: a language model trained on a huge amount of text, the kind providers sell.
The front-page document of a software project, explaining what it is and how to use it.
The standing instructions sent first with every request, telling the model what it is for. Bexendale's shop policy plays that part.
One program between your apps and the providers that holds the keys, budgets and logs (a6e01). Build Night X5 adds caching to it.
The course's hands-on build of cost and speed through an LLM gateway: caching answers and prompts, and routing to cheaper models.
Information about a person who can be identified from it, such as what they pawned and when it is due.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012. Its retention limitation obligation says not to keep personal data longer than its purpose needs.
The Data Protection Trustmark, Singapore's certification run by IMDA, its Infocomm Media Development Authority, showing that an organisation handles personal data well.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A control A.8.10, information deletion, asks that information be deleted when no longer required.

atWork: Look for an assistant that saves its answers and serves them again by meaning. It is a common pattern, and a common failure: a support assistant answering one customer's question about their order with another customer's saved answer, because where is order 81530 and where is order 81503 look almost the same to an embedding. Ask four things. Which questions are tied to one person or one record, and what key are their answers saved under: does it include the order number, the account or the user, or only the words? How was the threshold chosen, and on which labelled pairs? Is every hit logged with both questions and the score, and does anyone read a sample? And where do the tokens go: is a long fixed system prompt sent on every request, and are the calls close enough together for prompt caching to pay? Build Night X5, cost and speed through an LLM gateway, is where you build this: the gateway is the one place every request passes, so it can hold the answer cache, with exact keys for anything tied to a user and meaning-based matching only for general questions, and mark the fixed prefix for prompt caching. Standards-readiness note: if your cache stores answers tied to a person, those saved answers are personal data. If you operate under Singapore's PDPA or hold or seek DPTM certification, the retention limitation obligation means keeping them no longer than their purpose needs, so give them a short life and a way to delete them, and keep the user's identity in the key so they are never served to someone else. If you are certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control A.8.10, information deletion, expects stored information to be deleted when no longer required, and a cache is stored information. Deciding the keys and the lifetimes in the first design is far cheaper than finding personal answers in a shared cache during an audit.

recall.prompt: Your online shop's support assistant saves its answers and sends a saved one whenever a new question scores at least 0.92 against it by meaning. A customer asks where order 81530 is and is told the delivery date of order 81503. What went wrong, and how would you change the caching?

keyIdeas.idea: An answer tied to one customer's order must never be served for a different question by meaning
Use an exact key that includes the order number for those questions, or don't cache them
Similarity can't separate numbers that differ by a swap, so no threshold fixes it

recall.model: The cache matched two different questions because they read almost the same: the order numbers differ only by swapped digits, a sliver of the text, so the similarity score is high. Raising the line won't fix it; no threshold can separate them without also throwing away good hits, because a score says how alike two questions are, not whether they share an answer. An answer tied to one customer's order belongs to that order and must never be served for a different question by meaning. For those questions use an exact key that includes the order number and the customer, or don't cache them at all. Keep meaning-based matching only for general questions, like delivery times or returns, and log every hit with both questions and the score.

recall.prompt: A full call is 10,000 units: a 9,000-token fixed policy, and 1,000 units of question and answer. With prompt caching, the policy is read at 0.1 times the input price. What does a call that reads the cached policy cost?
recall.why: The policy costs 9,000 x 0.1 = 900 units when read from the cache, and the question and answer still cost their 1,000: 1,900 in all, 0.19 of a full call. 12,250 is a five-minute cache write: 9,000 x 1.25 + 1,000.

recall.prompt: Your app sends the same 6,000-token instructions at the start of every request, and requests arrive about once every 20 minutes, day and night. A colleague turned on prompt caching with the default settings. A month later the bill is slightly higher. Why, and what would you do?

keyIdeas.idea: The default life is five minutes, so the saved start has gone before the next request comes
Every call then pays to save it again, and a save costs more than normal input
Count the gaps: use the one-hour life, bring calls closer together, or turn it off

recall.model: Prompt caching only saves money when a request arrives while the saved start is still kept. The default life is five minutes, refreshed each time it is read, and your requests come every 20 minutes, so it has expired every time. Each call therefore saves the instructions again, and a write costs more than normal input, a quarter more for the five-minute life, so the bill rose. Count the gaps between calls first. Here, the one-hour life would work: it costs twice the input price to save, but nearly every call would then read the 6,000 tokens at about a tenth. If calls were hours apart, I would turn it off.

recall.prompt: Bexendale's week: 300 questions. Which plan gives no answer about another ticket and the lowest cost per question?
options: Meaning for everything at 0.95: 36 hits, 0.88 a question
Exact repeats only: 9 hits, 0.97 a question
Exact keys for tickets, meaning for the rest, policy cached for one hour: 75 hits, 0.28 a question
Meaning at 0.90, emptied at each shift change: 72 hits, 0.76 a question
recall.why: Emptying at each shift change still sends three answers about another ticket, tonight's among them. The other three send none, and the one-hour policy cache cuts each model call from 1.00 to 0.19 when it reads: 201 reads and 24 saves over 225 calls, 0.28 a question.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. No ticket has had another ticket's answer since, and the bill is about a third of what it was. But on 14 January the gold price jumped overnight. The policy is updated every morning with the day's price per gram, and from 09:00 to 16:00 the assistant told 38 customers yesterday's price: What do you pay for gold today? matched a general question saved at 17:20 the day before, at 0.97.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why were 38 customers given yesterday's price, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The saved answer was built from the old policy; when the source changes, answers built on it must go
Put the policy's version or date in the key, so a new policy can't match old answers
Answers that carry a live number should be looked up fresh or kept only a short time

coldCase.model: The cache did what it was told: the question matched one saved at 17:20, and that answer was built from the old policy, with yesterday's price in it. When the policy changes, every answer built on it is out of date, so the cache must be cleared, or the answers invalidated, the moment the new policy goes in. The cleanest way is to put the policy version in the key: an answer saved under yesterday's policy can then never match a question asked under today's. And an answer that carries a live price shouldn't come from a saved answer at all: look up the price fresh for each question, or keep such answers for a short life, minutes, not a day.
